title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 12.4.1 Writing: Guided Composition (Diary)

PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A diary is a personal record of what you did and how you felt. In this sub-strand you will name the parts of a diary, read a sample about caring for the environment, and write an entry in the right format. You will also see how a diary can help you remember, plan and write more clearly.

## Strand 12.0: Clean Environment
Sub-strand 12.4.1: Writing: Guided Composition (Diary)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the components of a diary for effective writing
b) write a diary in the right format for effective communication
c) adopt the use of diaries in our day-today lives

## What this sub-strand covers
• Diary

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we keep a record of what we do?
2. What information do we record?

## Core competencies
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: These competencies are manifested when the learner comes up with their own diary and displays it for the rest of the class members.
• Digital Literacy: This is achieved as learner ably manipulates digital devices when searching for information on how to write a diary from electronic resources.

## Values
• Responsibility: This is inculcated as the learner applies their diary in their day-to-day operations.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Self-esteem: The learner’s self-esteem is enhanced as they search for information on how to write a diary and apply it in their writing of a diary.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner applies the knowledge of writing a diary to learning of the same concept in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 12.0 Clean Environment, Sub-strand 12.4.1 Guided Composition: Diary

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: The parts of a diary entry

LESSON 1: THE PARTS OF A DIARY ENTRY
====================================

## What you will learn
• Name the components of a diary entry.
• Find those parts in a sample.
• Say what kind of information a diary records.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the components of a diary for effective writing

## Introduction
At the end of a busy day the details blur. A diary keeps them. It is not a composition for a stranger. It is a dated note to yourself about what happened and how you felt.

## Notes
### The components
A diary entry usually has these parts.

- The date, so you know which day you are writing about. Include the day and the date, such as Saturday, 3 May.
- A greeting: Dear Diary,
- The body, written in the first person. Use I, me, my and we. Tell the events in the order they happened. The past tense is usual, because the day has already happened.
- Feelings. A diary is more than a list of jobs. Say whether you were tired, proud, worried or glad.
- A closing with your name.

You do not need speech marks around the whole entry. You do need capital letters and full stops, because a diary is still careful writing.

### A sample to label
Saturday, 3 May

Dear Diary,

This morning our class cleaned the compound. I swept the path with a broom, and my friend pulled paper out of the drain. The work was hot, and at first I felt tired. Then we watered the young trees. I felt proud when the teacher said the grass looked green and tidy. Tomorrow I will remind the class to put fruit peels in the pit, not in the drain.

Amina

The date is Saturday, 3 May. The greeting is Dear Diary. The body tells two jobs in order, sweeping and then watering, and it includes feelings: tired, then proud. The last sentence looks ahead. The name Amina closes the entry. This is a sample for the classroom, not a report that these events happened to a particular person on that date.

### What we record
Record actions, places, people who helped, and feelings. Leave out unkind stories about other children. If the entry will be displayed, choose events you are happy for the class to read. A private diary at home can hold more personal thoughts, and you may keep that one to yourself.

The date matters because later you can see what changed. The first person matters because the diary is your record, not a story about a stranger.

## Key words
• diary — a personal written record of what you did and felt on a certain day
• entry — one dated piece of writing in a diary
• first person — writing with I, me, my and we
• greeting — the opening words, such as Dear Diary

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Name the five components in Amina's sample.

Working:
1. Look at the top, the opening, the middle, the feelings and the end.

Answer: The date, the greeting Dear Diary, the body of events, the feelings, and the name at the end.

### Example 2
Why is 'I swept the path' better in a diary than 'A girl swept the path'?

Working:
1. A diary is the writer's own record.
2. I is the first person.

Answer: Because a diary uses the first person. The writer is recording their own day.

## Activity: Label a sample diary
You will need: A copy of the sample entry, Coloured pencils
1. Read the sample alone, then compare it with a partner.
2. Mark the date, the greeting, one event, one feeling and the closing name in different colours.
3. Discuss whether the events are in order.
4. List three kinds of information you would record after a clean-up at your own school.

## Practice
1. What do you write at the very top of a diary entry?
2. Which greeting fits a diary?
3. Name two feelings in the sample.
4. Why might you leave a private worry out of an entry you will display?

## Summary
• A diary entry has a date, a greeting, a first-person body, feelings and a name.
• Events are written in order, usually in the past tense.
• Display only what you are happy for others to read.

### Answers to practice
1. The day and the date.
2. Dear Diary,
3. Tired and proud.
4. Because a displayed entry will be read by the class, so you choose events you are willing to share.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Writing an entry in the right format

LESSON 2: WRITING AN ENTRY IN THE RIGHT FORMAT
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Plan events in order before writing.
• Write a diary entry with all the components.
• Check person, tense and feelings.

Curriculum outcomes: b) write a diary in the right format for effective communication

## Introduction
The format is a frame. Your day supplies the picture inside it. If you plan three events in order, the entry will not jump from afternoon back to morning without warning.

## Notes
### Plan on a scrap of paper
Draw five boxes: date, greeting, events, feelings, name.

In the events box, number what happened. For a clean environment day you might write:

1. I collected rubbish into the bin.
2. I cleared dry leaves from the drain.
3. I watered the trees near the gate.

Add a feeling to one of them: I was worried because the drain was blocked, then glad when the water ran.

### Write the entry
Move the plan into sentences. Stay in the first person. Use the past tense for finished actions. You may use one future sentence at the end for what you will do next, as the sample did.

Monday, 12 May

Dear Diary,

After school I walked around our compound with two friends. First I picked up paper and put it in the bin. The drain by the kitchen was full of leaves, so we cleared it together. I felt worried when I saw the blocked drain, but I was glad when the water flowed. Tomorrow I will bring a brush so we can scrub the step as well.

Hassan

Check the frame. Date, greeting, ordered events, feelings, name. The word I appears several times. So and but join ideas without starting a new story.

### Common slips
- Forgetting the date, so the entry could belong to any day.
- Writing he or she about yourself.
- Using tomorrow's tense for the whole day: 'I will sweep' when you mean you already swept. Say 'I swept'.
- Listing unkind nicknames. Write about the work and your own feelings instead.

When the entry is neat, you may type it or copy it for display. Share the device fairly if the class has only one.

## Key words
• format — the set arrangement of parts in a piece of writing
• past tense — the verb form for an action that has already happened, such as swept or cleared
• plan — a short list of ideas in order, made before you write in full

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Rewrite this line in the first person and the past tense: Hassan will clear the drain.

Working:
1. The diary writer says I.
2. A finished action uses the past: cleared.

Answer: I cleared the drain.

### Example 2
The plan is: watered trees, then ate lunch, then swept. The draft says, 'I swept, and before that I had lunch, but first I watered the trees.' What is the clearer order?

Working:
1. Follow the plan from first to last.
2. Do not make the reader sort the time words.

Answer: First I watered the trees. Then I ate lunch. After that I swept.

## Activity: Write and display an entry
You will need: Exercise books, A sample diary to compare, A digital device if the class has one to share
1. List three things you did, or could honestly do, to keep a place clean. Put them in order and add one feeling.
2. Write a full diary entry with the date, Dear Diary, the body and your name.
3. Swap with a partner and check the five components.
4. Copy a neat version or type it, and display the entries you are willing to share.

## Practice
1. Put these events in a clear written order: I watered the trees. I picked up paper. I washed my hands.
2. Correct the tense: Dear Diary, Tomorrow I swept the compound.
3. What is missing? 'I cleared the drain and went home. Asha'
4. Write one diary sentence that includes a feeling about planting a tree.

## Summary
• Plan the events in order, then write them in the first person.
• Include the date, greeting, feelings and your name.
• Use the past tense for actions that are already finished.

### Answers to practice
1. Example: First I picked up paper. Then I watered the trees. After that I washed my hands.
2. Example: Dear Diary, Yesterday I swept the compound. or Today I swept the compound.
3. The date and the greeting Dear Diary are missing. A feeling would also strengthen the entry.
4. Example: I felt proud after I planted a tree beside the gate.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Why a diary is worth keeping

LESSON 3: WHY A DIARY IS WORTH KEEPING
======================================

## What you will learn
• Give reasons for keeping a diary.
• Use an entry to notice a habit and plan a next step.
• Start a simple routine you can continue.

Curriculum outcomes: c) adopt the use of diaries in our day-today lives

## Introduction
One entry shows a single day. A week of entries shows a pattern. You may discover that you remember the bin on Monday and forget it by Thursday. The diary makes that pattern visible.

## Notes
### What a diary can do
A diary helps you remember. Days at school are full, and a clean-up that felt important can fade. The date brings it back.

A diary helps you notice habits. If three entries say the drain was blocked, you can see a repeated problem and tell an adult, or you can plan to clear it earlier.

A diary helps you plan. The line 'Tomorrow I will bring a brush' is a promise you can check the next day. Did you do it? The next entry can answer.

A diary also makes you a better writer. You practise the first person, the past tense, order and feelings in a form short enough to finish.

### A second sample, one day later
Sunday, 4 May

Dear Diary,

I looked back at yesterday's page. I had promised to talk about the fruit peels. This morning I told my brother, and we put the peels in the pit instead of the drain. I felt happy because I had kept my word. The compound was still tidy. I will check the drain again on Monday.

Amina

This entry only works because Saturday's entry existed. The diary has become useful, not only decorative.

### A routine you can keep
You do not need a long entry every night. Three or four sentences on the days when something matters are enough. Keep the book in the same place. Write the date first so you never wonder when the page was written.

Use your diary for any part of life, not only cleaning: a match, a kind action, a mistake you repaired. If you write about the environment often, you will have a record of how you care for your compound and neighbourhood.

Keeping a diary is a habit of responsibility. You watch your own actions honestly and decide what to repeat.

## Key words
• habit — something you do often, sometimes without a fresh decision each time
• routine — a regular way of doing something
• record — writing that keeps information so it is not forgotten

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Saturday's entry says, 'Tomorrow I will bring a brush.' What can Sunday's entry do with that sentence?

Working:
1. A later entry can check a promise.
2. Say whether the action happened and how you felt.

Answer: It can record whether you brought the brush, and how the job went.

### Example 2
Three entries say the class bin was overflowing. What pattern do you see, and what is one next step?

Working:
1. The same problem returns.
2. A next step should be practical.

Answer: The bin is not emptied often enough. A next step is to empty it each afternoon or to ask for a collection rota.

## Activity: A diary you can continue
You will need: A notebook to use as a diary, Printed or electronic samples of diary pages
1. Look at two sample entries and discuss how the second one follows the first.
2. Search a book or a page your teacher provides for one more tip about diary writing, and share it.
3. Write today's entry about something you did for a clean environment, using the full format.
4. At the end, add one sentence beginning 'Tomorrow I will'. Keep the notebook for the next school day and check that promise.

## Practice
1. Give two reasons for keeping a diary.
2. How does a date make a diary more useful?
3. What should you do with a promise such as 'Tomorrow I will check the drain'?
4. Why is a short regular entry better than one very long entry you never repeat?

## Summary
• A diary helps you remember, notice habits, plan and practise writing.
• Later entries can check the promises of earlier ones.
• A short, regular, honest entry is a useful habit.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: to remember, to notice habits, to plan the next day, to practise writing.
2. You can tell which day an event happened and see how things changed later.
3. Check it in the next entry and record whether you did it.
4. A regular entry builds a record and a habit. One long entry is easy to abandon.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 12.4.1 WRITING: GUIDED COMPOSITION (DIARY)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which set lists the main parts of a diary entry?
   A. Title, rhyme, chorus
   B. Date, greeting, body, name
   C. Question, answer, map
   D. Address, stamp, postmark

2. The usual greeting is
   A. Dear Sir
   B. Dear Diary,
   C. Once upon a time
   D. Yours faithfully

3. A diary body is usually written in
   A. the first person
   B. the third person only
   C. no person at all
   D. rhyme without sentences

4. Which line belongs in a diary about a finished clean-up?
   A. I swept the path and felt proud.
   B. Once there was a magic broom.
   C. The end of chapter one.
   D. Question: what is a bin?

5. Which entry uses the past tense correctly for a finished action?
   A. I cleared the drain.
   B. I will cleared the drain.
   C. I clearing the drain yesterday.
   D. Clear I the drain.

6. What is missing from this entry? 'Dear Diary, I watered the trees. I felt glad. Omar'
   A. The date
   B. The verb
   C. The name
   D. The feeling

7. Why record feelings as well as events?
   A. Feelings replace the date
   B. They show what the day meant to you
   C. A diary cannot include events
   D. Feelings must be unkind

8. A line that says 'Tomorrow I will empty the bin' is useful because
   A. it is a plan you can check later
   B. it removes the need for a date
   C. it must be a proverb
   D. it ends the diary forever

9. Why is a diary worth keeping?

10. What should you do if an entry will be displayed in class?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 12.4.1 WRITING: GUIDED COMPOSITION (DIARY)
========================================

1. B. Date, greeting, body, name
   A diary entry needs a date, a greeting, a body and the writer's name.

2. B. Dear Diary,
   Dear Diary is the greeting taught for this form.

3. A. the first person
   The writer uses I, me and my.

4. A. I swept the path and felt proud.
   It uses I, a finished action and a feeling.

5. A. I cleared the drain.
   Cleared is the past tense of a finished action.

6. A. The date
   There is a greeting, a feeling and a name, but no date.

7. B. They show what the day meant to you
   Feelings make the entry a personal record, not only a list.

8. A. it is a plan you can check later
   The next entry can say whether you kept the promise.

9. It helps you remember what you did, notice habits, plan the next step and practise clear writing.
   Those uses make the diary part of ordinary life.

10. Write about events and feelings you are willing for other learners to read, and leave private worries for a diary you keep to yourself.
   A displayed diary is shared writing, so the content should be suitable to share.

2. A next step should be practical.

Answer: The bin is not emptied often enough. A next step is to empty it each afternoon or to ask for a collection rota.

## Activity: A diary you can continue
You will need: A notebook to use as a diary, Printed or electronic samples of diary pages
1. Look at two sample entries and discuss how the second one follows the first.
2. Search a book or a page your teacher provides for one more tip about diary writing, and share it.
3. Write today's entry about something you did for a clean environment, using the full format.
4. At the end, add one sentence beginning 'Tomorrow I will'. Keep the notebook for the next school day and check that promise.

## Practice
1. Give two reasons for keeping a diary.
2. How does a date make a diary more useful?
3. What should you do with a promise such as 'Tomorrow I will check the drain'?
4. Why is a short regular entry better than one very long entry you never repeat?

## Summary
• A diary helps you remember, notice habits, plan and practise writing.
• Later entries can check the promises of earlier ones.
• A short, regular, honest entry is a useful habit.

### Answers to practice
1. Any two: to remember, to notice habits, to plan the next day, to practise writing.
2. You can tell which day an event happened and see how things changed later.
3. Check it in the next entry and record whether you did it.
4. A regular entry builds a record and a habit. One long entry is easy to abandon.

questions.question: Which set lists the main parts of a diary entry?
questions.explanation: A diary entry needs a date, a greeting, a body and the writer's name.

questions.question: The usual greeting is
questions.explanation: Dear Diary is the greeting taught for this form.

questions.question: A diary body is usually written in
questions.explanation: The writer uses I, me and my.

questions.question: Which line belongs in a diary about a finished clean-up?
options: I swept the path and felt proud.
Once there was a magic broom.
questions.explanation: It uses I, a finished action and a feeling.

questions.question: Which entry uses the past tense correctly for a finished action?
questions.explanation: Cleared is the past tense of a finished action.

questions.question: What is missing from this entry? 'Dear Diary, I watered the trees. I felt glad. Omar'
questions.explanation: There is a greeting, a feeling and a name, but no date.

questions.question: Why record feelings as well as events?
options: They show what the day meant to you
questions.explanation: Feelings make the entry a personal record, not only a list.

questions.question: A line that says 'Tomorrow I will empty the bin' is useful because
options: it is a plan you can check later
it removes the need for a date
questions.explanation: The next entry can say whether you kept the promise.

questions.question: Why is a diary worth keeping?
questions.answer: It helps you remember what you did, notice habits, plan the next step and practise clear writing.
questions.explanation: Those uses make the diary part of ordinary life.

questions.question: What should you do if an entry will be displayed in class?
questions.answer: Write about events and feelings you are willing for other learners to read, and leave private worries for a diary you keep to yourself.
questions.explanation: A displayed diary is shared writing, so the content should be suitable to share.
